topic: Developing a Peptide Separator for Separation of TNT
title: Developing a Peptide Separator for Separation of TNT
authors_text: Lauren Ng, Harrison Heath, Aaron Beyea, Robert Bozic, Scott Banta and Alan West
abstract: Long term monitoring of waste disposal sites for Munitions Constituents, MCs, using the Environmental Protection Agency Method 8330A, high performance liquid chromatography, is a costly analytical technique for which there is not a current comparable alternative. This has inspired research and development of fast, low cost techniques to detect parts per billion concentrations of MCs such as such as 2,4,6-TNT as well as other MCs in ground water. In collaboration with the U.S. Army Engineer Research and Development Center in Vicksburg, MS, Columbia University Department of Chemical Engineering and the Department of Chemistry and Life Science at the United States Military Academy have on-going research efforts combining electrochemical engineering, microfluidics, and protein engineering with a goal of developing engineering fundamentals to enable in-situ detection of MCs. The current focus is on development of methods that will selectively detect concentrations of an MC from roughly nanomolar quantities to reliably detectable levels via electrochemical methodologies using a peptide separation unit in line with an electrochemical sensor. Research during this Advanced Individual Development Program was done on developing a method using a Quartz Crystal Microbalance (QCM) and on Isothermal Titration Calorimetry (ITC) to study binding interactions between TNT and peptides engineered to bind TNT.

topic: Piperazine Degradation in a Post Combustion Carbon Capture Pilot Plant
title: Piperazine Degradation in a Post Combustion Carbon Capture Pilot Plant
authors_text: Dias Kazbekuly, Paul T. Nielsen and Gary T. Rochelle
abstract: Piperazine Degradation in a Post Combustion Carbon Capture Pilot Plant Dias Kazbekuly, Paul T Nielsen, Gary T Rochelle Texas Carbon Management Program McKetta Department of Chemical Engineering The University of Texas at Austin Abstract Amine scrubbing is a proven technology used to separate carbon dioxide and other acid gases from natural gas. It can also potentially be used to capture CO 2 from post combustion flue gas from coal and natural gas fired power plants. However, post combustion flue gas will contain oxygen and other contaminants that will degrade the solvent. Thermal degradation of the solvent can also occur in the high-temperature solvent-regenerating stripper. Concentrated aqueous piperazine has been proposed as an alternative to the baseline monoethanolamine solvent due to its increased resistance to thermal and oxidative degradation. Liquid solvent samples were collected and analyzed from a post combustion carbon capture pilot plant, operated with a slipstream of flue gas from a coal-fired power plant. The campaign was performed at stripper operating temperatures of 120 °C and 155 °C and used 40 wt % piperazine solvent. During the period of the campaign held at 120 °C, formate, the most significant liquid phase oxidation product, accumulated at a rate of 56 μmol/(kg*hr). The rate increased to 170 μmol/(kg*hr) when the temperature was increased. No significant accumulation of thermal degradation products was observed. The rate of stainless steel metal ion accumulation due to corrosion increased significantly from 0.14 to 1.0 µmol/(kg*hr) after the temperature of the stripper was increased. Sulfate and nitrate from the absorption of SO x and NO x in the flue gas accumulated at a rate of 25 and 16 μmol/(kg*hr), respectively. N-nitroso-piperazine (MNPZ) is a carcinogenic byproduct that can form from the reaction of piperazine with NO 2 absorbed from the flue gas. MNPZ is thermally unstable and will degrade at stripper conditions, limiting the maximum concentration in the solvent. After a steady state of 7 mmol/kg was achieved at 120 °C, the temperature was raised to 155 °C, and the MNPZ concentration dropped rapidly to a new steady state of 2 mmol/kg. Both these observations comply with the values predicted using a kinetic model developed for MNPZ decomposition.

topic: Improving the Design of a Milli-Fluidic Device
title: Improving the Design of a Milli-Fluidic Device
abstract: Through the course of my research this summer, I improved the design and fabrication of milli-fluidic devices as well as their ability to perform liquid-liquid extraction (LLE). Many chemical processes require a separation of resultant compounds in order to yield a specific product. For example, pharmaceutical companies rely on compound separation to recover pharmaceutical molecules from an organic environment by extracting them into an aqueous stream. Called liquid-liquid extraction, the process of transferring a solute from one liquid phase into another is based on the interaction and behavior of two immiscible fluids. Yet, LLE commonly occurs on a large scale, which can lead to low separation efficiency and low product yield due to incomplete separation of the two liquid phases. Some existing separation methods include evaporation, centrifugation, or filtration, but these techniques can degrade the molecule of interest and are susceptible to loss of product. For these reasons, LLE on a milli-fluidic level is more appealing because it caters to the extraction of small volumes of costly solutes. Hence, a major objective of my summer research was to improve the design of existing milli-fluidic prototypes to boost the usefulness and appeal of using such devices. The design and fabrication of milli-fluidic devices at the start of my research were impractical and ineffective, resulting in unstable devices. The devices held too many components that could vary from device to device. Through my research, I improved the design of milli-fluidic devices by simplifying the manufacturing process and increasing their effectiveness. My efforts to accomplish this were centered on modifying the fabrication technique and materials of construction. Such modifications include replacing the needles in the device with larger diameter tubing and utilizing different diameter tubing throughout the device to control its internal pressure. I tested and compared device prototypes based on their ability to stabilize an aqueous/organic interface and separate an aqueous/organic emulsion. The construction of a milli-fluidic device involves using a laser cutter to print an acrylic top and bottom piece, in which the bottom piece contains two input channels, a larger fluid compartment where the aqueous/organic interface occurs, and two effluent channels. A needle is adhered to the upper left channel, 14-gage tubing in the upper right channel, and 18-gage tubing in the lower left and right channels. “Loctite Plastic Bonding System” adhesive is used to secure the tubing needles in the channels. The two acrylic pieces are then secured to each other with six screws, six nuts, and twelve washers. A PEG solution is injected into the fluid compartment, and ultraviolet light is used to cure a layer of PEG hydrogel inside of the device. Holding the device perpendicular to the ultraviolet light is crucial in forming a smooth layer, which is important in maintaining laminar flow within the device. Overall, the improvements I have made to the design and fabrication process of milli-fluidic devices has allowed for an increase in manufacturing efficiency, structural consistency between devices, and performance.

topic: Efficient Liquid Liquid Extraction By Emulsion Formation and Separation in Robust Milli-Fluidic Devices
title: Efficient Liquid Liquid Extraction By Emulsion Formation and Separation in Robust Milli-Fluidic Devices
abstract: This project investigates the feasibility of increasing transport between phases during liquid liquid extraction by the use of milli-fluidic devices by increasing contact time. In traditional liquid liquid extraction, separation by gravity limits contact time of emulsions. Milli-fluidic devices allow this contact time to be extended and controlled, increasing predictability and efficiency. The examined milli-fluidic process includes the formation of an emulsion, over which the contact time is controlled by tubing length, and an emulsion separation device. The emulsion separation device utilizes the attraction of the aqueous phase to a hydrogel lining within the channel in order to stabilize colaminar flow of the aqueous and organic phases. This process allows for the efficient separation of streams at a controlled time in order to increase mass transfer. These devices handle greater liquid flows than previously recorded for milli-fluidic devices, increasing their potential application to industrial processes. In industrial settings, milli-fluidic devices can reduce the volumetric flow required of the phases in order to carry out the process and obtain the desired amount of mass transfer. Lowering the volume required for the process has an important impact potential in industries which deal with high value products. This study examines a system of water, octanol, and FD&C red.

topic: Investigation of Membrane Selectivity for the Demineralization and Purification of High Value Fermentation Products
title: Investigation of Membrane Selectivity for the Demineralization and Purification of High Value Fermentation Products
authors_text: Alfonso Puente, Alexander M. Lopez and Jamie A. Hestekin
abstract: Electrodialysis with ion exchange membranes is finding novel and broader applications. It represents one of the most versatile separation methods with a great potential of application in the dairy industry, desalination of salt water, and the demineralization of whey, sugars, and organic acids. Electrodialysis can also be used to separate fermentation products, which are used in the food, cosmetic, and perfume industries. However, fermentation broths contain strong metal contaminants and metabolic products that need to be removed during product purification. This study focused on the purification and demineralization of high value fermentation broth products through electrodialysis with ion exchange membranes. Membrane selectivity was studied in order to selectively remove ions in a multi component solution. It was determined that the separation coeficients for butyrate over acetate for Ameridia PC SA-ED, Ameridia A0352, and Fumasep FAS membranes were 0.37, 0.61, and 0.68 with current efficiencies at 79% , 91%, and 50% respectiviely. From this research, we have determined that it is viable to selectively separate and purify fermentation broths through electrodialysis.

topic: Crystallization of β-Glycine from Water Via Monodisperse Droplet Evaporation
title: Crystallization of β-Glycine from Water Via Monodisperse Droplet Evaporation
authors_text: Anna Maassel and Ryan C. Snyder
abstract: There is great potential for technological advancement in the pharmaceutical and food industries as a result of data from modern research on crystallization. Properties of particles and crystals, such as morphology and polymorphism, have substantial effects on the performance of the final product. The ability to control these properties and understand their result as a function of the underlying chemistry and the formation process is a modern challenge. Moreover, the ability to control these properties during particle formation rather than manipulating them via post-processing steps allows for improved processing. This research examines the formation of crystalline glycine, the smallest amino acid, through monodisperse droplet evaporation. Specifically, this work demonstrates the effects of different solvents combined on the morphologies and polymorphs of glycine that are produced. Previous research suggests that the metastable alpha polymorph forms by crystallization of glycine from pure water solutions. Only when more complex chemistry is used is the beta polymorph of glycine produced. Some such methods that have formed the beta polymorph include crystallization from an organic cosolvent, a change in pH, crystallization through freeze drying, and crystallization in polymer nanorods. Contrary to past results, this work demonstrates the production of beta glycine from pure water solutions by evaporating small droplets. Additionally, this research also presents the resulting morphologies of glycine using this technique from pure water, water/acetone solvent mixtures and water/ethanol solvent mixtures obtained by scanning electron microscopy (SEM).

title: Methane Adsorption in MOF
abstract: Sara Alkazzaz Abstract -Methane Adsorption Using MOF AICHE Student Conference – Poster Competition Storage and Transportation of -the main component of natural gas- has been one of the difficulties of natural gas utilization. Adsorbed natural gas has developed to be a safer alternative technology in which the natural gas is adsorbed by a porous material such as activated carbon or MOF. This technology is preferred because it is obtained at low pressure 5-35 bar and room temperature. It is also economically favorable because it does not require the use of complex and expensive liquefactions equipment, also the natural gas should not be compressed to high pressure 200-248. This research studies the capacity of adsorption of methane in MOF at three different temperatures 15, 25 and 35 C. Isotherm data were generated. Using adsorbing unit filled with 40 g of MOF , the adsorber has a volume of 124.55 ml. Mass balance was developed to measure the number of methane moles that was adsorbed into the surface of MOF. Calculations were done using Matlab and Toth equation to generate adsorption isotherms. Temperature, the physical properties of MOF such as packing density and micropore area play important role in determining the amount adsorbed of methane .

topic: Regeneration of Carbon Based Adsorbents through Thermal and Microwave Treatment
title: Regeneration of Carbon Based Adsorbents through Thermal and Microwave Treatment
authors_text: Jordan Benton-Smith, Anthony B. Dichiara and Reginald E. Rogers Jr.
abstract: There has been increasing interest in the use of single-wall carbon nanotubes (SWCNTs) for water treatment purposes. Recent studies have looked into using a hybrid of carbon nanotubes and graphene combined in a ratio of 2:1 as a more effective adsorbent than single-wall carbon nanotubes alone. The problem with using these adsorbents is that they are expensive and cannot practically be replaced often like the traditional adsorbent, activated carbon. This study examines a method of regenerating the hybrid papers exhausted with 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid (2,4-D) through heat and microwave treatments. Optical (absorption) spectroscopy is used to measure the solution concentrations and adsorption rates. Samples are prepared from a stock solution of 100 µg 2,4-D/mL and are tested at concentrations of 65 µg/mL, 55 µg/mL, 45 μg/mL, 35 μg/mL, and 25 µg/mL. Adsorption isotherms are generated from solution concentrations after a saturation period of 1 day showing the maximum adsorption capacity of the adsorbents. Saturated papers then undergo heat treatment at 550°C for 5 minutes followed by microwave treatment at 1200 watts for 15 minutes. The regenerated hybrid papers are then saturated in the same way. A comparison of the maximum adsorption capacities shows that the desorption process was effective in completely removing the 2,4-D as well as improving the adsorbent material to achieve a 5% increase in capacity. Adsorption kinetics of the adsorbent also improved from a linear short time adsorption to an exponential short time adsorption.

topic: Synthesis of Stimuli-Responsive Polymer Brushes on Cellulose Membranes for the Reduction of Protein Fouling on Membranes Used for Field-Flow Fractionation
title: Synthesis of Stimuli-Responsive Polymer Brushes on Cellulose Membranes for the Reduction of Protein Fouling on Membranes Used for Field-Flow Fractionation
abstract: Synthesis of Stimuli-Responsive Polymer Brushes on Cellulose Membranes for the Reduction of Protein Fouling on Membranes used for Field-Flow Fractionation Field-Flow Fractionation (FFF) is an analytical technique used to separate macromolecules such as polymers, nanoparticles, and proteins. The technique employs a flowing fluid with a laminar velocity profile inside a small, ribbon-like channel. The analyte is separated in the channel via two competing forces. The first is applied by the user (electric, thermal, hydraulic, etc.) and causes the analyte injected into the channel to sink to the bottom. This defines the type of FFF, as well as the kind of samples the technique can separate. The opposing force is molecular diffusion, which causes the analyte to rise from the bottom according to a physical parameter such as size. Each particle diffuses away from the channel wall towards the center of the flowing fluid, reaching faster layers of liquid in the channel. Thus, the particles are separated by reaching different fluid velocity layers. In Cross-Flow Field-Flow Fractionation (AF4), the applied force is another fluid crossing the laminar separation stream. To allow the crossing of fluids, a membrane must be present at the bottom of the channel which allows the crossing liquid to exit, but not the analyte. The addition of a membrane into AF4 also introduces a challenge associated with membranes used in other separations. This problem is called membrane fouling, which is simply the adsorption of matter to the surface of a membrane. The cellulose membranes used in AF4 are prone to fouling by proteins; a problem my research addresses. Polymer brushes are end-attached polymer chains which are covalently linked to a surface. The grafting of polymer brushes from or to a surface allows the tuning of surface properties without altering the overall bulk properties of the material. Thus, in order to reduce membrane fouling by proteins in AF4, poly(N-isopropylacrylamide) (PNIPAM), a temperature-responsive polymer shown to reversibly adsorb and desorb to proteins, was grafted from the cellulose membranes used in the separation technique. Using Atom-Transfer Radical Polymerization (ATRP) and a novel scale-up procedure which can be completed in-lab, a method for the synthesis of PNIPAM brushes on cellulose membranes used in AF4 has been developed. The effects of these brushes on membrane fouling are currently under investigation. If successful, this study may lead to a solution to membrane fouling in AF4 which can be applied to other separations.

topic: Hybrid Zeolitic Imidazolate Frameworks: Controlling Framework Porosity and Functionality By Mixed-Linker Synthesis of ZIF-8-90
title: Hybrid Zeolitic Imidazolate Frameworks: Controlling Framework Porosity and Functionality By Mixed-Linker Synthesis of ZIF-8-90
authors_text: Catherine Blad, Fereshteh Rashidi, Christopher W. Jones and Sankar Nair
abstract: Hybrid zeolitic imidazolate frameworks (ZIF), a class of metal-organic frameworks with zeolitic topologies, exhibit synthetically tunable properties such as microporosity and chemical functionality. The ZIF-8 linker (2-methylimidazole, 2-MeIM) and the ZIF-90 linker (carboxaldehyde-2-imidazole,OHC-IM) are incorporated into the hybrid framework of ZIF-8-90, creating a combination of different ligands in differing relative quantities. This study focused on improving ZIF-8-90 synthesis methods to increase ZIF-8 inclusion and tune the crystal size by changing linker ratio and using different Zn precursors. These hybrids were synthesized using a nonsolvent induced crystallization technique (NSIC). This study showed the effects of various ZIF-90 and ZIF-8 linkers’ ratio on the crystal size and composition of the ZIF-8-90 hybrid framework. 1 H NMR showed that the ZIF hybrid frameworks preferentially include OHC-IM over 2-MeIM due to ZIF-90 linker’s lower solubility in the nonsolvent. Using Zn precursors with lower disassociation constants might increase ZIF-90 solubility in the non-solvent phase and then enhancing ZIF-8’s ability to be included in the hybrid structure. XRD demonstrated the ZIF-8-90 unit cell volume increased with OHC-IM loading while maintaining the same cubic crystal structure. Therefore, higher ZIF-8 incorporation results in smaller unit cell volumes. The ZIF-8-90 hybrid introduces an opportunity for post-synthetic modification by incorporating a functional group into the hybrid network. By increasing ZIF-8 incorporation, the hybrid may have new applications for hydrocarbon separations. Alterations in the chemical and structural properties enable hybrid ZIFs to be viable candidates for a variety of gas separations.

topic: Flux Modulations and Separations with Temperature and pH Responsive Membranes
title: Flux Modulations and Separations with Temperature and pH Responsive Membranes
abstract: Flux Modulations and Separations with Temperature and pH Responsive Membranes K. Waldrop*, L. Xiao, D. Bhattacharyya Krysta.waldrop@gmail.com, li.xiao@uky.edu, DB@uky.edu Dept. of Chemical and Materials Engineering University of Kentucky Lexington, Kentucky Temperature responsive materials have proven to be very useful in bioseparation, water treatment, and drug delivery. By functionalizing a membrane with a temperature-responsive polymer, tunable flux can be achieved quickly with minimal energy consumption, making a valuable tool for the aforementioned fields. Poly-N(isopropyl acrylamide) (PNIPAM) is a temperature-responsive polymer which has drawn much attention in recent years. At temperatures below 32°C (the lower critical solution temperature, or LCST) PNIPAM exists in a hydrophilic state, causing the polymer chains to absorb water and swell, but, above the LCST, the polymer becomes hydrophobic, collapsing the polymer chains. When PNIPAM is functionalized within membrane pores, the temperature responsive behavior allows for control of the effective pore size. The goal of this research was to study the permeation and rejection behavior with changing temperature of PNIPAM functionalized polyvinylidene fluoride (PVDF) membranes. PVDF membranes were functionalized with PNIPAM using free radical in situ polymerization. The flux and dextran rejection (2,000,000 MW) were studied at 2.1 bar and temperatures of 30°C and 34°C. Tests confirmed that below LCST the flux was 1.44 LMH and 95% of dextran was rejected, and above the LCST flux increased to 9.72 LMH and only 30% of the dextran was rejected. PNIPAM functionalized full-scale PAA-PVDF membranes were also developed to observe both temperature and pH effects on flux and sodium sulfate rejection (100ppm). Below LCST, functionalized full-scale membranes rejected 50% of the sodium sulfate with a flux of 13 LMH at a pH of 4 and at a pH of 8, 90% of the sodium sulfate was rejected with a flux of 10 LMH. Above the LCST, sodium rejection was 25% with flux at 81 LMH at a pH of 4 and a flux of 52 LMH with an 82% rejection was observed at a pH of 8. It could be concluded that an increase in temperature led to an overall increased flux but decreased rejection. This work was supported by NIEHS-SRP

topic: Oxidative Study of Amino Polymer Supported Adsorbents for CO2 Capture
title: Oxidative Study of Amino Polymer Supported Adsorbents for CO2 Capture
authors_text: Thomas T. Chen and Christopher W. Jones
abstract: Increasing levels of CO 2 in the atmosphere, currently at 400 ppm, have been correlated with global climate change. Of the methods to capture CO 2 , solid adsorbents are a promising option because of their ease of synthesis and use and high adsorption capacities. For this study, branched poly(ethylenimine) (PEI) and poly(allylamine) (PAA) supported on mesoporous γ-alumina are evaluated for their oxidative stability under various conditions. Adsorbents containing PEI are composed of primary, secondary, and tertiary amines, whereas PAA contains only primary amines. A thermal oxidation study of PEI impregnated alumina demonstrates a reduction in degradation of PEI under humid conditions versus dry conditions. Using 21% O 2 , PEI experiences an 89.5% and 37.7% reduction in CO 2 capacity under dry conditions at 110 o C and 70 o C; whereas under humid conditions a 70.1% and 33.4% reduction in CO 2 capacity is observed at the same temperatures. Next, the oxidative stability of PEI and PAA are compared. Under the harshest conditions, 110 o C and 21% O 2 , it is observed that the PEI impregnated adsorbents undergo considerable degradation, and degradation of the PEI is reduced with a lower temperature and O 2 concentration, 70 o C and 5% O 2 . In contrast, the use of PAA impregnated alumina showed much increased oxidative stability with only a 10.9% reduction in CO 2 capacity after treatment with 21% O 2 at 110 o C. Use of FTIR, FT-Raman, and 13 C NMR spectroscopy to characterize the oxidized sorbents shows key differences between the PEI and PAA samples. Of most interest is the carbonyl (C=O) peak, which is present in the oxidized PEI but not PAA samples. This is consistent with previous work that demonstrated that secondary amines, such as those within PEI, contribute to the lack of oxidative stability of amine-based sorbents, which PAA does not contain. Thus PAA can be used in development of adsorbents with increased oxidative stability for use in CO 2 capture.

topic: Synthesis and Characterization of Room-Temperature Ionic Liquid Copolymers As Membranes for CO2 Capture
title: Synthesis and Characterization of Room-Temperature Ionic Liquid Copolymers As Membranes for CO2 Capture
abstract: Copolymer membranes have been synthesized using an imidazole-based ionic liquid monomer and a neutral analogue. The CO2 permeability and selectivity with respect to N2 and CH4 of these membranes have been experimentally characterized. Additionally, the physical swelling of these polymers in organic solvents and acidic solutions has been measured and correlated to the ratio of ionic to neutral monomer constituents. The overall goal of this project is to explore the physical properties of complex ionic liquid membranes with potential uses in industrial gas separations or solvent absorption.

topic: Adsorption Properties of Single-Wall Carbon Nanotube- Graphene Hybrid Papers for the Removal of Organic Compounds from Aqueous Environments
title: Adsorption Properties of Single-Wall Carbon Nanotube- Graphene Hybrid Papers for the Removal of Organic Compounds from Aqueous Environments
authors_text: Tyler J. Sherwood, Reginald E. Rogers Jr. and Anthony B. Dichiara
abstract: Graphene and single-wall carbon nanotubes (SWCNT) have been a primary focus for the development of a variety of new applications, including improvements in water filtration and wastewater treatment via adsorption. Removal of a model organic compound, 1-pyrenebutyric acid (PBA), by graphene and SWCNTs are compared to the commonly used activated carbon to show their effectiveness at removing organic compounds from aqueous environments. Studies are done using graphene, in house and commercial SWCNTs, and a hybrid mixture of graphene and commercial SWCNTs. Using a UV/Visible/NIR spectrophotometer, the absorbance of PBA is measured under short time (< 3 hours) to understand the adsorption kinetics (rates) and long time ( >4 weeks) to study equilibrium behavior (adsorption capacities). Adsorption of 2,4-dichlorophenoxyacetic acid is also studied due to its common use as an herbicide. Untreated graphene shows twice the adsorption rate of PBA as activated carbon and approximately the same adsorption rate of 2,4-D. For the kinetics studies the hybrid papers performed best with 25 times the adsorption of activated carbon and graphene, which is double the adsorption rate of commercial SWCNTs by themselves. In house SWCNTs show approximately 20 times the adsorption rate of activated carbon and graphene for both PBA and 2,4-D. Commercial SWCNTs show approximately 10 times the adsorption capacity of activated carbon and graphene for PBA while in house SWCNTs and hybrid papers show approximately 15 times the adsorption capacity of activated carbon and graphene. Further studies using a mixture of in house SWCNTs and graphene and the use of different adsorbates will help to show the effectiveness of single-wall carbon nanotubes, graphene, and their hybrid forms as viable everyday adsorbents for filtration processes.
